sense: energy put into something, hard work

evidence: Cic. Fam. 14.18.2: maximē autem date operam ut valeātis
Plaut. Poen. 332: et oleum et operam perdidī
Traupman 97: make an effort to be on time, dā operam ut tempestīvē adsīs
Traupman 308: it’s (not) worth the effort, pretium operae (nōn) est
Traupman p. 110: operam dō ut (nē) (+ subjunctive)
terms.comment: Operam dare ut, to make an effort to, to see to it that; operam perdere, to waste one’s effort; operae pretium est, it is worth the effort. Lewis & Short: opera “supposes a free will and desire to serve”, where opus is the work itself.

evidence: Liv. 21.4.5: nūllō labōre aut corpus fatīgārī aut animus vincī poterat
Cic. de Or. 2.210: magnō illa labōre … esse parta
terms.comment: Effort as toil, often tiring: magnō labōre, with great effort.

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, deponent; with ut and the subjunctive
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.42: ēnītī et contendere dēbet quam maximē possit, ut vincat
terms.comment: “Make an effort” is often a verb: ēnītī, operam dare, or cōnārī (see try).
In Suetonius the phrase means to regard a thing as important, not to take pains over it; for “take pains to” classical Latin says operam dare ut (above).

phrases.latin: maximē autem date operam ut valeātis, sī nōs vultis valēre
phrases.english: above all, make every effort to keep well, if you want us to be well

phrases.latin: sī, quantum operae sūmpsistī ut tuus pistor bonum faceret pānem, ejus duodecimam philosophiae dedissēs, ipse bonus jam prīdem essēs factus
phrases.english: if you had given philosophy a twelfth of the effort you spent getting your baker to make good bread, you would have become good yourself long ago

phrases.latin: Tum pol ego et oleum et operam perdidī.
phrases.english: Then, by heaven, I’ve wasted my lamp oil and my effort.

phrases.latin: factūrusne operae pretium sim … nec satis sciō
phrases.english: whether I shall be doing something worth the effort … I am not quite sure
